catalog_quote: 5.2 Stress. Stress in Dobu is non-phonemic in 2-syllable words occurring on the penultimate syllable. In many 3-syllable words it falls on the antepenultimate. In some such 3-syllable words, stress fluctuates; in others it is fixed. /ona/ ['ona] 'word' /tana/ ['tʰana] 'basket' /pou/ ['pʰou] 'egg' /tetela/ [tʰe'tʰela] 'story' /bagula/ ['bagula] 'garden' /tamagu/ ['tʰamagu/tʰa'magu] 'my father'. In words of more than 3 syllables, the stress patterns can be regarded as combinations of 2- or 3-syllable segments, with the characteristic stress patterns of such. ... Two-syllable words: CV.V 'po.u 'egg'; CV.CV 'ni.ma 'hand'; V.CV 'a.ba 'creeper type'. Three-syllable words: V.CV.V e'ta.i 'harvest'; V.CV.CV e'ta.la 'python'; CV.CV.CV gi'da.ba 'stick insect'; CV.V.CV 'ma.i.na 'bad smell'. new_statements.relation_note: The catalog lists Dobu with an empty rule and there are no existing stress statements; the excerpt supplies a placement (penultimate, with alternating secondary stresses) that the catalog lacks, so it refines rather than contradicts. Confidence is low because the placement is read off stress-marked transcriptions rather than from a stated rule, and because only 5 of the paper's 24 pages were opened. The complete PDF exists as an open attachment on SIL's archive (https://www.sil.org/resources/archives/23690) but its download link https://www.sil.org/system/files/reapdata/15/48/09/154809813581974116139856854434427719122/Dobu_Phonemics.pdf is behind an automated-access block Turnstile challeng…
new_statements.rule_in_words: The pages read contain no sentence stating the stress rule; but every phonetic transcription in the phoneme statements carries stress marks, and in all of them the stress mark sits on the penultimate syllable of the word (ba.ba.'ba.na, ko.ko.'la.ka, te.'te.la, de.'doi, si.'si.si, ne.'nai, yu.'yu.na, o.la.'o.la, u.we.'nu.nu, a.sa.ko.'wa.si), with additional (secondary) marks on every second syllable counting leftward from the penult ('ba.ba.'ba.na, 'lo.li.'ma.na, 'u.we.'nu.nu, a.'sa.ko.'wa.si, ʔa.'sui.'nua.'nua). The text also refers to 'unstressed syllables' and 'unstressed positions' as the sites of vowel reduction ([a]~[ʌ], [ɔ] after labialized consonants), which presupposes a word-stress contrast. Penultimate primary stress with alternating secondary stress is therefore what the excerpt shows; the paper's explicit statement (probably in a suprasegmental section on pp. 83-91) was not read.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Transcriptions mark a second stress on alternate syllables to the left of the penult (e.g. ['baba'bana], ['loli'mana], ['uwe'nunu], [a'sakʰo'wasi], [ʔa'sui'nua'nua]); the excerpt does not label it as secondary in words.
new_statements.exceptions: None in the pages read; four-syllable words with a diphthong-like sequence (esaesae [e'sae'sae], asuinuanua) are marked consistently with the same pattern.
new_statements.identity_note: Both works describe Dobu proper (SIL subject language Dobu [dob]); Lithgow's 1975 grammar excerpt on the same archive.org item places the language on Dobu and Sanaroa Islands and the adjacent coasts of Fergusson and Normanby Islands and calls it the D'Entrecasteaux lingua franca. No dialect is singled out in the pages read.
